# Method {#sec-method}

```{r}
#| label: p4-method-setup
#| include: false
m_flb_B1 <- cf(p4_arm_grid, "B1", "mkt")
m_flb_B2 <- cf(p4_arm_grid, "B2", "mkt")
```

## The two-stage conditional logit

For runner $i$ in race $j$,

$$
V_{ij} \;=\; \beta_{\text{mkt}} \log P^{\text{mkt}}_{ij}
           \;+\; \beta_{\text{mod}} \log P^{\text{mod}}_{ij},
\qquad
\Pr(\text{$i$ wins race $j$}) \;=\;
  \frac{e^{V_{ij}}}{\sum_{k \in j} e^{V_{kj}}} ,
$$ {#eq-blend}

where $P^{\text{mkt}}$ is a market-implied win probability and
$P^{\text{mod}}$ a model win probability. Benter used this to combine a
fundamental model with the public odds [@benter1994]. Race is the choice
set, as in every conditional logit in this series, and the fit is by
maximum likelihood over the observed winners. There is no intercept: an
alternative-invariant constant cancels in the softmax, so the three-part
`{mlogit}` formula `won ~ ... | 0 | 0` used in papers 1 to 2b carries
over unchanged.

Both probabilities are already normalised within race, so @eq-blend is a
weighted geometric combination of them, renormalised. A coefficient of 1
uses a source as stated; above 1 sharpens it toward the favourite, below
1 flattens it. $\beta_{\text{mod}}$ is the output.

## Why $\beta_{\text{mkt}}$ is not pinned at 1

Fixing $\beta_{\text{mkt}} = 1$ would assert that the market's
probabilities need no sharpening or flattening before use. If that is
wrong, the likelihood has only one free parameter left to correct it
with, and part of $\beta_{\text{mod}}$ becomes a recalibration of the
market rather than a measure of the model. The bias runs upward, and
worst where the market is worst calibrated — which is where a large
$\beta_{\text{mod}}$ would otherwise look most like a finding. Both
coefficients are therefore free.

In the two starting-price blends, one per model source, the market
coefficient comes out at `r fmt_b(m_flb_B1$estimate)` and
`r fmt_b(m_flb_B2$estimate)`, close to 1.

## Three prices

| Arm | Price | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Pre-race racecard forecast | The forecast price as published ahead of the race, from Smartform's daily feed of forthcoming racecards. Available at bet time. |
| **B** | Industry starting price | The settled market at the off, and the price the series already uses for its market baseline and its backtests. |
| **C** | Archived racecard forecast | The forecast price as recorded in Smartform's results archive. Nominally the same quantity as arm A, and not identical to it (@sec-appx-provenance). |

: The three prices. {#tbl-price-columns}

Arms A and B are the contrast the paper is about: an early price against
the settled one. Arm C exists because the archived value is the obvious
one to reach for and does not match the pre-race one; it supports the
attenuation bracket in @sec-discussion. @sec-appx-provenance gives the
schema detail and the evidence.

All three arms are fitted on one race set — the intersection over the
three prices — because a comparison of $\beta_{\text{mod}}$ across arms
is void if the arms sit on different races.

## Market probability construction

Each price becomes a win probability by the proportional overround
adjustment the series has used since paper 1 §5.1: implied probability
$1/\text{price}$ per runner, renormalised to sum to one over the field.
Paper 4 does not restate that arithmetic in code; the function it calls
is checked against the series' existing implementation by a standing
gate, which rebuilds the stored `win_market` column of paper 3's test
predictions from raw starting prices and requires agreement to
$10^{-12}$. Observed agreement is exact.

Normalisation is over the runners that started, which is the field the
model scores. The forecast price is struck against the declared field,
before withdrawals are known, so a race that loses runners shows a lower
overround here than the one the bookmaker struck. Renormalisation is
unaffected: it rescales to sum to one either way.

Races are dropped whole where any runner lacks a usable price; dropping
individual runners would change the normalisation for the rest of the
field. Both probabilities are floored at $10^{-6}$ before taking logs.

## Two model sources, neither refitted

$P^{\text{mod}}$ comes from paper 2b's exploded conditional logit and
paper 3's gradient-boosted tree ensemble, read from the stored test-set
predictions of their own papers. Neither is refitted or retuned. The two
sit on identical runner sets over identical races, which is what makes
the comparison between them paired.

## Where the blend is fitted

$\beta_{\text{mod}}$ is only meaningful on out-of-sample model
probabilities. Papers 2b and 3 were fitted on the training split, so
their training-split probabilities are optimistic and the blend would
read that optimism as information the market lacks. The blend therefore
sits on the held-out races — the one place this paper sets aside the
series' training-split-only convention, which @sec-data keeps. A
two-parameter model on roughly a thousand races carries negligible
overfitting risk; the same could not be said of the models supplying
$P^{\text{mod}}$.

The test universe is split chronologically in two. Test-A, the earlier
half, is fitted first; test-B was held back. The boundary is a calendar
date, so the split is reproducible against an exact date, as the series'
2012-12-30 train/test cutoff is; races on the cutoff date go to test-A.
@sec-results reports what test-B was spent on.
